newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition readies for lengthy protests.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition readies for lengthy protests.

text.p: Serbia's opposition said on Saturday it was preparing for a marathon series of protests against election fraud after President Slobodan Milosevic showed no sign of bowing to their demands or to Western pressure.

The opposition, whose daily rallies on the streets of Belgrade have lasted since its victories in mid-November local elections were annulled by the ruling Socialists, said it might also boycott Serbian presidential elections next year.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition has said the Serbian government's admission on Friday of the opposition's partial victory in disputed polls was insufficient. It has vowed to keep demonstrating until all its successes were recognised.
But ruling Socialists on Saturday snubbed redoubled calls from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe to recognise all Zajedno's election triumphs.

The socialist controlled election commission in Serbia's second largest city of Nis ordered a rerun of the vote in 17 electoral districts, in clear defiance of a court order to acknowledge Zajedno won the vote in the southern city.
The OSCE on Friday officially endorsed Zajedno's claim it won in 15 of Serbia's biggest cities, including Belgrade.
The Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic had earlier accepted some Zajedno victories in a letter to the OSCE.
Aimed at defusing criticism, the letter backfired when organisations at home and abroad issued damning responses.
The United States slammed Belgrade's "hollow assurances" of commitment to democracy and Zajedno called the letter a pack of lies.

"We will continue protests until the same time next year if it takes. Not that it will, given the rising amount of support we are getting from the population," said Milan Bozic, political advisor to Vuk Draskovic, one of Zajedno leaders.

He was among opposition figures who believe the autocratic Milosevic's authority is crumbling under pressure from the protesters and gestures of dissent from the army, Church and even from within his feared police forces.
But a Democratic party spokesman said the police were also bracing for the long haul.

"Since the authorities have set up pre-fabricated buildings in Belgrade to house the police... there is no doubt the SPS (ruling Socialist Party) has decided to keep them there for a long time," Slobodan Vuksanovic said.

Zoran Djindjic, one of Zajedno's leaders, said if Milosevic did not show he was ready to make concessions, Zajedno would not only boycott the presidential elections but also withdraw its members from parliament.

Serbian presidential elections are due by the end of the year. After a landslide victory last November for the federal parliament, the ruling socialists hinted that Milosevic would hold them as early as in March to capitalise on his popularity.
But the defeat at the local elections and ensuing mass protests have forced Milosevic to delay the election until the end of the year, analysts say.
Tens of thousands of whistle-blowing supporters protested in a Belgrade square for the 47th consecutive day on Friday with fresh protests due on Saturday.

The protest erupted into an ear-splitting noise at 7:30 p.m. as Belgraders leaned from windows and balconies to blow whistles and bang pots to "drown" out the nightly news bulletin on state television, which they accuse of slanted coverage.
